rewrites.title: Genetic dissection with AP-1 component perturbation
rewrites.description: Repeat the stop-and-wait and thermoremanent-style protocols in cells with inducible dominant-negative c-Jun (TAM67), c-Fos or JunB knockdown, and in cells lacking specific AP-1 partners, rescuing with wild-type constructs. If the memory signature disappears specifically when AP-1 function is lost and returns on rescue, AP-1 is necessary for the memory rather than just correlated with it.

rewrites.title: Parental histone inheritance at AP-1 enhancers
rewrites.description: Label pre-existing H3 or H3.3 with a SNAP/Halo tag, pulse with AP-1 stimulus, then chase through one or two divisions and use quantitative CUT&Tag to measure whether old versus newly synthesized histones are retained at primed enhancers. Preferential retention of old histones at AP-1-bound sites would suggest that memory is carried by histone recycling rather than by the transcription factor itself.

rewrites.title: Phosphorylation-site knock-ins as a durable mark
rewrites.description: Generate Fos and Jun phosphosite knock-ins (phospho-null and phospho-mimetic at ERK/JNK-dependent sites) and run phosphoproteomics across a pulse-washout-rechallenge series. If a long-lived phospho-state carries information after total protein has returned to baseline, the phospho-mimetic and phospho-null lines should differ in second-exposure responses even when first-exposure responses match.

rewrites.title: Single-cell test of AP-1 accessibility as a predictor of memory state
rewrites.description: Analyze public single-cell multiome (scRNA plus scATAC) datasets from infection, tumor, or inflammation models to ask whether the AP-1 motif accessibility score in a cell predicts its membership in a memory-like versus terminally differentiated state. Check whether the association holds after conditioning on lineage markers and on the cell's stimulation history.

rewrites.title: Optogenetic AP-1 pulse-pattern test of memory
rewrites.description: Use optogenetically controlled FOS/JUN dimerization or nuclear translocation to deliver defined pulse patterns (duration, frequency, amplitude), then measure whether past pulse history alters later transcriptional output and enhancer opening after a long rest. This separates memory encoded by AP-1 dynamics from memory encoded by upstream signaling.

rewrites.title: Protein turnover measurement and degradation-resistant AP-1 variants
rewrites.description: Measure Fos and Jun protein half-lives and phosphorylation states across the post-stimulus interval with pulse-chase labeling, to identify whether a long-lived AP-1 pool exists. Then express ubiquitin-resistant or phospho-mimetic Fos mutants that extend protein lifetime and test whether memory duration scales with protein stability rather than with transcription.

rewrites.title: Targeted epigenome editing at memory-associated AP-1 enhancers
rewrites.description: Use dCas9 fused to KRAB, DNMT3A, or TET1 catalytic domains to erase or write chromatin marks at a few individual AP-1-bound enhancers identified as memory-associated, while leaving AP-1 binding itself intact. If editing these specific enhancers abolishes or creates memory without changing AP-1 occupancy, the chromatin mark rather than the factor is the causal memory element.

rewrites.title: Acute AP-1 degradation after the stimulus ends
rewrites.description: Prime cells (e.g., macrophages, fibroblasts, or neurons) with a stimulus, then use degron tags (dTAG/AID) on FOS, JUN, and ATF family members at different times after priming. Compare whether the enhanced secondary response persists when AP-1 is removed during the rest period, which separates AP-1 as the memory carrier from AP-1 as only the initiator.

rewrites.title: Lag-dependent re-stimulation decay curves
rewrites.description: Prime cells with a defined AP-1 stimulus, then re-challenge after variable rest intervals filled with neutral or non-AP-1 stimuli. Measure the secondary induction of AP-1 target genes (RNA-seq or qPCR) and fit decay models: pure activation decay predicts exponential loss of the boost, while true memory predicts a persistent plateau that outlasts the transcription factor's own occupancy.

rewrites.title: Time-resolved occupancy and accessibility tracking
rewrites.description: Run CUT&RUN or CUT&Tag for AP-1 members, together with ATAC-seq and H3K27ac, at several points: during the stimulus, at hours and days after washout, and after re-stimulation. This shows whether AP-1 stays bound at primed enhancers or whether accessibility persists after AP-1 has left.

rewrites.title: Perturbation of the AP-1 positive-feedback loop with mathematical modeling
rewrites.description: Rewire or break the FOS/JUN autoregulatory loop (e.g., mutate TRE sites in the JUN/FOSL1 promoters, or add a synthetic feedback) and fit dynamical models to dose-response and hysteresis measurements. Observing bistability or hysteresis that is lost when the loop is cut would test whether AP-1 network topology itself encodes memory.

rewrites.title: Retention-interval and spaced-versus-massed stimulation test
rewrites.description: Give cells one stimulus pulse, wait a variable retention interval, then give an identical test pulse and quantify enhanced response (faster or larger AP-1 target induction by scRNA-seq or live reporters) as a function of interval length and of massed versus spaced stimulation pulses. A genuine memory system should show a quantifiable retention decay constant and a greater effect of spaced than massed stimulation, and knocking down specific Fos/Jun family members should selectively flatten that curve.

rewrites.title: Acute AP-1 degron with memory-persistence readout
rewrites.description: Using endogenous FOS/JUN family dTAG/AID degrons, transiently stimulate cells (e.g., with inflammation or injury), then degrade AP-1 at defined times after the stimulus is removed. Measure whether enhancer accessibility and faster re-induction persist for weeks without AP-1, which would separate AP-1's role in establishing memory from its role in maintaining it.

rewrites.title: In vivo rechallenge with cell-type-specific AP-1 knockout
rewrites.description: Delete Jun or Fosb conditionally in a defined population (for example, monocytes or tissue-resident macrophages) after a primary inflammatory or stimulatory insult, then rechallenge weeks later and measure the secondary response with scRNA-seq and chromatin profiling. Comparing the memory response in knockout and wild-type animals tests whether AP-1 is required for memory in vivo, not just in culture.

rewrites.title: Optogenetic pulse-pattern encoding of memory
rewrites.description: Use light-inducible AP-1 (optoFos/optoJun) to deliver trains that vary pulse number and inter-pulse interval, then measure the magnitude of the second response. Dependence on interval rather than total dose would show that AP-1 encodes temporal history, not just its last state.

rewrites.title: Dissecting AP-1 sites by locus-specific editing and epigenome writing
rewrites.description: At endogenous memory-associated enhancers, mutate AP-1 motifs, or use dCas9 to place or remove acetylation, methylation and SWI/SNF (BAF) recruitment, with and without AP-1 present. Testing which of these changes is necessary and sufficient for a primed re-response shows whether the memory lies in AP-1 binding itself or in downstream chromatin marks it leaves behind.

rewrites.title: Reversible cell-cycle block during the priming window
rewrites.description: Prime cells with a defined AP-1 stimulus while holding them in G1 with a reversible CDK4/6 or CDC7 inhibitor, or in G2/M with a comparable block, then release and test re-induction. If memory is lost or diluted without DNA replication, it depends on replication-coupled chromatin dilution rather than on a stable, non-replicative state.

rewrites.title: Tracking AP-1 through mitosis
rewrites.description: Tag endogenous Jun or Fos with HaloTag or a similar label for live imaging across cell divisions, and run CUT&Tag on sorted mitotic cells to see whether AP-1 stays bound to memory enhancers during mitosis. Then test whether daughter cells inherit accessibility and the primed response. Mitotic retention would support mitotic bookmarking as a memory mechanism.

rewrites.title: Primed versus naive re-stimulation with phase-specific AP-1 degradation
rewrites.description: Give a first stimulus, rest cells for days to weeks until FOS/JUN levels return to baseline, then re-stimulate and compare transcriptional kinetics and amplitude with naive cells (RNA-seq, nascent-RNA 4sU-seq). Test causality by acutely degrading AP-1 (dTAG/AID) only during the priming window versus only during the rest period, to determine when AP-1 is needed to establish versus maintain the memory.

rewrites.title: Faster re-induction after return to baseline with phase-specific AP-1 degradation
rewrites.description: Prime cells, wait until the transcriptional response fully returns to baseline, then re-stimulate and measure response latency and amplitude. Degrading AP-1 selectively during the interval between stimuli versus during re-stimulation separates a role for AP-1 in storing the memory from a role in executing the response.
